title: Experimental Biology II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 100L second-semester biology practical curriculum: classification/identification keys, plant and animal external morphology, field ecology techniques (quadrats, transects, capture-recapture), enzyme and photosynthesis/respiration experiments, water relations of tissues, biological drawing conventions, and specimen preservation. Distinct from BIO107 (microscopy, lab safety, staining, food tests).

questions.question: A dichotomous key used to identify an unknown specimen works by presenting the user with:
options: A series of paired, contrasting statements, each leading to another pair or to an identification
A single list of all possible species names in alphabetical order
A photograph library to be matched by eye only
A random sequence of measurements to be averaged
questions.correct_answer: A series of paired, contrasting statements, each leading to another pair or to an identification
questions.explanation: A dichotomous key branches through successive either/or choices about observable features until the specimen is identified.

questions.question: In binomial nomenclature, when writing a scientific name by hand in a laboratory notebook, the correct convention is to:
options: Underline the genus and species names separately since italics cannot be handwritten
Write both names entirely in capital letters
Place the species name before the genus name
Enclose the whole name in quotation marks
questions.correct_answer: Underline the genus and species names separately since italics cannot be handwritten
questions.explanation: Because handwriting cannot show italics, each word of a scientific name is underlined separately to indicate what would otherwise be italicised.

questions.question: During a field classification exercise, a specimen is described as having a leaf with a single, undivided blade. This leaf is correctly classified as:
options: Simple
Compound
Pinnate
Palmate
questions.correct_answer: Simple
questions.explanation: A simple leaf has one continuous, undivided lamina, unlike a compound leaf whose blade is divided into leaflets.

questions.question: A student observes a leaf whose blade is divided into leaflets arranged in pairs along a central axis (rachis), with a terminal leaflet. This venation/leaf arrangement is best described as:
options: Pinnately compound
Palmately compound
Simple with parallel venation
Simple with reticulate venation only
questions.correct_answer: Pinnately compound
questions.explanation: In a pinnately compound leaf, leaflets are arranged on both sides of a common rachis, as in leaves of many legumes.

questions.question: When distinguishing a monocotyledonous leaf from a dicotyledonous leaf in a practical class, the monocot leaf is typically identified by:
options: Parallel venation
Reticulate (net-like) venation
A well-developed petiole and net veins
Compound leaflets only
questions.correct_answer: Parallel venation
questions.explanation: Monocot leaves characteristically show veins running parallel to each other along the length of the leaf, while dicots usually show branching, net-like venation.

questions.question: In a root system practical, a tap root system is distinguished from a fibrous root system by:
options: The presence of one main root that is thicker than its lateral branches
Having many roots of roughly equal thickness arising from the stem base
Growing only in aquatic plants
Lacking root hairs entirely
questions.correct_answer: The presence of one main root that is thicker than its lateral branches
questions.explanation: A tap root system has a single dominant primary root, typical of dicots, whereas a fibrous system has many similarly sized roots, typical of monocots.

questions.question: During external examination of a preserved toad (Bufo) specimen, the parotid glands, which secrete a defensive toxin, are located:
options: Behind the eyes on the dorsal surface of the head
On the ventral surface of the abdomen
Inside the buccal cavity
At the tip of the digits
questions.correct_answer: Behind the eyes on the dorsal surface of the head
questions.explanation: The parotid glands appear as raised, oval swellings just behind each eye and secrete bufotoxin as a predator defence.

questions.question: In an external morphology study of the cockroach (Periplaneta americana), the body is correctly divided into three main regions called the:
options: Head, thorax, and abdomen
Cephalothorax, abdomen, and telson
Head, mantle, and foot
Anterior, medial, and posterior segments
questions.correct_answer: Head, thorax, and abdomen
questions.explanation: Like other insects, the cockroach body is organised into a head, a three-segmented thorax bearing the legs and wings, and an abdomen.

questions.question: When setting up a quadrat sampling exercise to estimate plant population density in a field, the main purpose of using a quadrat is to:
options: Sample a defined, representative area so results can be scaled to the whole habitat
Kill unwanted specimens before counting
Measure the exact age of every plant present
Replace the need for any counting of individuals
questions.correct_answer: Sample a defined, representative area so results can be scaled to the whole habitat
questions.explanation: A quadrat marks out a fixed sample area; counts within it are used to estimate density or frequency over the larger habitat.

questions.question: To reduce bias when placing quadrats during a field survey, students are advised to:
options: Position quadrats at random, for example using random number coordinates
Always place quadrats where plants look most abundant
Use only one quadrat placed at the entrance of the field
Choose quadrat positions after seeing what is inside them
questions.correct_answer: Position quadrats at random, for example using random number coordinates
questions.explanation: Random placement avoids the observer unconsciously choosing sites that are unusually rich or poor in the organism being studied.

questions.question: A line transect differs from a quadrat survey in that a line transect is used primarily to:
options: Record the organisms that touch or lie along a marked line, often to study a gradient across a habitat
Enclose a fixed square area for counting individuals
Measure the depth of soil at a single point
Trap flying insects only
questions.correct_answer: Record the organisms that touch or lie along a marked line, often to study a gradient across a habitat
questions.explanation: A transect line is laid across a habitat (e.g. from shore to inland) to record how species composition changes along an environmental gradient.

questions.question: In the capture-mark-recapture (Lincoln index) method for estimating animal population size, the formula used is:
options: Population size = (number marked in first catch x total number in second catch) / number marked recaptured in second catch
Population size = number marked in first catch + number caught in second catch
Population size = number marked recaptured / number marked in first catch
Population size = total area sampled divided by number of quadrats
questions.correct_answer: Population size = (number marked in first catch x total number in second catch) / number marked recaptured in second catch
questions.explanation: The Lincoln index estimates total population as (M x N) / R, where M is the first sample marked, N is the second sample size, and R is the number of marked individuals recaptured.

questions.question: For the capture-recapture method to give a reliable population estimate, a key assumption is that:
options: Marked individuals mix randomly back into the population and marks do not affect survival
No animal in the population may ever be caught more than once
The population size changes considerably during the study
Marking must be visible only under ultraviolet light
questions.correct_answer: Marked individuals mix randomly back into the population and marks do not affect survival
questions.explanation: The method assumes marked animals redistribute randomly and are neither more nor less likely to survive or be recaught, and that the population is closed during sampling.

questions.question: In an enzyme practical testing catalase activity using hydrogen peroxide and fresh liver tissue, the gas produced that is tested with a glowing splint is:
options: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Hydrogen
Nitrogen
questions.correct_answer: Oxygen
questions.explanation: Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen; the oxygen produced relights a glowing splint, confirming enzyme activity.

questions.question: In an experiment testing the effect of temperature on amylase activity using starch-iodine solution, a blue-black colour that fails to disappear at 80 degrees Celsius most likely indicates that:
options: The enzyme has been denatured by heat and can no longer break down starch
The enzyme is working faster than at lower temperatures
Iodine solution has evaporated
Starch has been fully converted to maltose
questions.correct_answer: The enzyme has been denatured by heat and can no longer break down starch
questions.explanation: High temperatures disrupt the enzyme's tertiary structure (denaturation), so it can no longer hydrolyse starch, and the blue-black starch-iodine colour persists.

questions.question: When designing a controlled enzyme experiment to test the effect of pH on amylase activity, the variable that must be kept constant across all test tubes is:
options: Temperature, substrate concentration, and enzyme volume
The pH of the buffer used in each tube
The colour of the indicator used
The time of day the experiment is performed
questions.correct_answer: Temperature, substrate concentration, and enzyme volume
questions.explanation: To isolate the effect of pH, every other factor that could affect reaction rate (temperature, substrate and enzyme amounts, timing) must be held constant.

questions.question: In the classic experiment to test a leaf for starch as evidence of photosynthesis, boiling the leaf in ethanol (water bath) before applying iodine serves to:
options: Remove chlorophyll so the iodine colour change can be clearly seen
Kill the leaf cells so photosynthesis stops immediately
Convert starch into glucose for easier detection
Sterilise the leaf surface
questions.correct_answer: Remove chlorophyll so the iodine colour change can be clearly seen
questions.explanation: Ethanol dissolves out the green chlorophyll pigment, leaving the leaf pale so the blue-black iodine-starch reaction is visible.

questions.question: In a destarching and starch-test experiment, a leaf is first kept in darkness for 24-48 hours before the light experiment begins in order to:
options: Remove any starch already stored in the leaf so results reflect only the treatment applied
Kill the leaf so it does not respire during the experiment
Increase the leaf's chlorophyll content
Prevent the leaf from wilting
questions.correct_answer: Remove any starch already stored in the leaf so results reflect only the treatment applied
questions.explanation: Destarching ensures any starch detected afterward resulted from photosynthesis during the actual experimental treatment, not from starch made earlier.

questions.question: Using the bubble-counting method with an aquatic plant such as Elodea (pondweed) to study photosynthesis, the number of bubbles released per minute is taken as an indirect measure of the rate of:
options: Oxygen production
Carbon dioxide absorption only
Water uptake by the roots
Chlorophyll synthesis
questions.correct_answer: Oxygen production
questions.explanation: The gas bubbles released by a submerged photosynthesising plant are largely oxygen, so counting them approximates the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.question: In a simple respirometer experiment using germinating seeds, soda lime (or KOH) is placed in the apparatus to:
options: Absorb the carbon dioxide produced, so any volume change reflects oxygen consumption
Absorb oxygen so only carbon dioxide is measured
Provide extra nutrients to the seeds
Prevent the seeds from germinating too quickly
questions.correct_answer: Absorb the carbon dioxide produced, so any volume change reflects oxygen consumption
questions.explanation: Soda lime absorbs the CO2 released during respiration, so the resulting drop in gas volume/pressure in the closed system measures oxygen uptake.

questions.question: In a respirometer set-up, a control tube containing glass beads instead of living seeds, treated identically otherwise, is included to:
options: Account for changes in volume caused by temperature and pressure fluctuations rather than respiration
Provide extra carbon dioxide for the experiment
Serve as food for the seeds
Speed up the reaction between soda lime and seeds
questions.correct_answer: Account for changes in volume caused by temperature and pressure fluctuations rather than respiration
questions.explanation: The control corrects for physical changes in gas volume due to atmospheric conditions, isolating the volume change actually caused by respiration.

questions.question: In the classic potato cylinder osmosis experiment, cylinders placed in distilled water gain mass mainly because:
options: Water moves into the potato cells by osmosis, since the cell sap has a lower (more negative) water potential than distilled water
Starch inside the cells is converted directly into extra water
Salts diffuse out of the water into the potato
The potato cylinders absorb oxygen from the water
questions.correct_answer: Water moves into the potato cells by osmosis, since the cell sap has a lower (more negative) water potential than distilled water
questions.explanation: Distilled water has a higher (less negative) water potential than the potato cell sap, so water enters the cells by osmosis, increasing mass.

questions.question: In the potato osmosis experiment, the concentration of external sucrose solution at which the potato cylinders show no change in mass approximates:
options: The solute (osmotic) concentration of the potato cell sap
The boiling point of the sucrose solution
The total volume of water in the beaker
The starch content of the potato
questions.correct_answer: The solute (osmotic) concentration of the potato cell sap
questions.explanation: At the concentration where no net water movement occurs, the external solution's water potential equals that of the potato tissue, revealing its internal solute concentration.

questions.question: In the water relations experiment, drying and reweighing each potato cylinder with blotting paper before and after immersion is important because it:
options: Removes surface water so that only the actual mass change of the tissue itself is measured
Prevents the potato from losing starch
Sterilises the surface of the cylinder
Increases the accuracy of the ruler measurement
questions.correct_answer: Removes surface water so that only the actual mass change of the tissue itself is measured
questions.explanation: Blotting removes water clinging to the surface, ensuring the recorded mass reflects water that has actually entered or left the tissue by osmosis.

questions.question: When making a biological drawing of a specimen in the laboratory, the accepted convention is to:
options: Use plain, continuous, single lines without shading, with labels connected by straight lines and a title stating magnification
Use heavy shading and colouring to make the drawing look realistic
Sketch freehand without labels to save time
Copy an image from a textbook rather than draw the actual specimen observed
questions.correct_answer: Use plain, continuous, single lines without shading, with labels connected by straight lines and a title stating magnification
questions.explanation: Standard biological drawing convention favours clean outline drawings, horizontal label lines that do not cross, and a title/magnification for scientific accuracy.

questions.question: In a scientific biological drawing, label lines are conventionally drawn:
options: As straight lines that do not cross one another, ending exactly at the structure identified
As curved arrows pointing away from the drawing
Only in a numbered list beside the diagram
As dotted lines crossing through the drawing
questions.correct_answer: As straight lines that do not cross one another, ending exactly at the structure identified
questions.explanation: Non-crossing straight label lines keep the drawing legible and ensure each label is unambiguously linked to its structure.

questions.question: To measure the length of a small specimen such as a snail shell precisely to a fraction of a millimetre, the most appropriate instrument in a biology laboratory is a:
options: Vernier caliper
Metre rule only
Beam balance
Hand lens
questions.correct_answer: Vernier caliper
questions.explanation: A vernier caliper allows precise measurement of small lengths, including internal, external, and depth dimensions, to a fraction of a millimetre.

questions.question: A quadrat frame commonly used in field ecology practicals in Nigerian universities is most often constructed with internal dimensions of:
options: 1 metre by 1 metre
10 metres by 10 metres
1 centimetre by 1 centimetre
100 metres by 100 metres
questions.correct_answer: 1 metre by 1 metre
questions.explanation: A 1 m x 1 m quadrat is a standard, practically manageable sampling unit for herbaceous vegetation and small invertebrate surveys.

questions.question: When a set of field measurements (for example, plant heights) is recorded, calculating the arithmetic mean is done by:
options: Summing all the recorded values and dividing by the number of measurements taken
Taking the largest value recorded
Subtracting the smallest value from the largest value
Multiplying all values together
questions.correct_answer: Summing all the recorded values and dividing by the number of measurements taken
questions.explanation: The mean is the sum of all observations divided by the total number of observations, giving a measure of central tendency for the data set.

questions.question: The range of a set of field data (for example, leaf lengths) is calculated as:
options: The largest value minus the smallest value
The sum of all values divided by their number
The most frequently occurring value
The middle value when data are ordered
questions.correct_answer: The largest value minus the smallest value
questions.explanation: The range is a simple measure of spread found by subtracting the minimum recorded value from the maximum recorded value.

questions.question: For long-term storage of an animal specimen for later dissection or display, a common preservative fluid used in the teaching laboratory is:
options: Formalin (dilute formaldehyde solution)
Concentrated hydrochloric acid
Pure distilled water only
Undiluted iodine solution
questions.correct_answer: Formalin (dilute formaldehyde solution)
questions.explanation: Formalin fixes tissue proteins and prevents decay, making it a standard preservative for zoological specimens used in teaching.

questions.question: When preparing a herbarium specimen of a flowering plant for a taxonomy practical, the correct first step after collection is to:
options: Press and dry the plant flat between absorbent sheets under moderate pressure
Boil the plant in water for ten minutes
Store the fresh plant directly in a sealed plastic bag indefinitely
Soak the plant in concentrated salt solution
questions.correct_answer: Press and dry the plant flat between absorbent sheets under moderate pressure
questions.explanation: Pressing and drying preserves the plant's flattened form and prevents fungal decay, which is essential before mounting a herbarium sheet.

questions.question: In a comparative practical exercise on floral structure, a flower described as 'actinomorphic' is one that:
options: Can be divided into two identical halves along more than one plane (radial symmetry)
Can only be divided into two identical halves along a single plane (bilateral symmetry)
Has no petals at all
Occurs only in wind-pollinated plants
questions.correct_answer: Can be divided into two identical halves along more than one plane (radial symmetry)
questions.explanation: Actinomorphic (radially symmetrical) flowers, like hibiscus, can be cut into identical halves along several planes, unlike bilaterally symmetrical (zygomorphic) flowers.

questions.question: During an insect mouthpart comparison practical, the cockroach's mouthparts are classified as the ancestral, generalised type known as:
options: Biting and chewing (mandibulate) mouthparts
Piercing and sucking mouthparts
Siphoning mouthparts
Sponging mouthparts
questions.correct_answer: Biting and chewing (mandibulate) mouthparts
questions.explanation: The cockroach retains simple mandibulate mouthparts adapted for biting and chewing solid food, considered the basic insect mouthpart type.

questions.question: In an ecological practical comparing two habitats, species richness refers to:
options: The total number of different species present in a given area
The total number of individual organisms present, regardless of species
The average body size of organisms in the habitat
The amount of rainfall recorded in the habitat
questions.correct_answer: The total number of different species present in a given area
questions.explanation: Species richness is simply a count of how many distinct species occur in the sampled area, distinct from abundance or diversity indices.

questions.question: When constructing a simple food chain from field observations of a pond ecosystem (algae, tadpole, small fish, heron), the correct trophic sequence is:
options: Algae to tadpole to small fish to heron
Heron to small fish to tadpole to algae
Tadpole to algae to heron to small fish
Small fish to heron to algae to tadpole
questions.correct_answer: Algae to tadpole to small fish to heron
questions.explanation: Energy flows from the primary producer (algae) through successive consumers, so the correct order runs producer, herbivore, secondary consumer, tertiary consumer.

questions.question: In a practical exercise identifying stem types, a stem that is green, soft, and non-woody is described as:
options: Herbaceous
Woody
Succulent only
Rhizomatous only
questions.correct_answer: Herbaceous
questions.explanation: Herbaceous stems lack extensive secondary (woody) growth and remain green and relatively soft throughout the plant's life.

questions.question: During dissection of an earthworm to study its external segmentation, the clitellum is significant because it:
options: Is a glandular, saddle-like structure involved in cocoon formation during reproduction
Is the mouth opening at the anterior end
Marks the position of the anus
Contains the worm's brain
questions.correct_answer: Is a glandular, saddle-like structure involved in cocoon formation during reproduction
questions.explanation: The clitellum secretes mucus and albumin to form the cocoon in which fertilised eggs develop, and its position helps identify anterior-posterior orientation.

questions.question: In a practical comparing seed types, a key external feature distinguishing a monocotyledonous seed (e.g. maize) from a dicotyledonous seed (e.g. bean) is:
options: The maize seed has one cotyledon while the bean seed has two
The maize seed has no seed coat while the bean seed does
The bean seed cannot germinate while the maize seed can
The maize seed lacks an embryo
questions.correct_answer: The maize seed has one cotyledon while the bean seed has two
questions.explanation: The defining difference between monocots and dicots, visible on dissecting the seed, is the number of cotyledons (seed leaves) present in the embryo.
